extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York / voters and ratifiers (1788)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative arguments and standards for structuring the federal House of Representatives: who may vote and hold office, appropriate term length and election frequency, rules for apportionment (including treatment of slaves), and the appropriate total size of the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of the electors
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those of the former are to be the same with those of the electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Convention fixed the qualifications of federal electors by reference to the standards already (or potentially) established in each State for their most numerous legislative branch — making the federal electors' qualifications conformable to State standards so as to be satisfactory to the States and safe for the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the right of suffrage as a constitutional article
rubrics_metrics.description: "The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution itself should define and establish the right of suffrage rather than leaving it to occasional regulation by Congress or discretionary regulation by State legislatures, because leaving it open would make the federal branch too dependent on State governments or on transient legislative discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of the elected (representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A representative of the United States must be of the age of twenty-five years; must have been seven years a citizen of the United States; must, at the time of his election, be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent; and, during the time of his service, must be in no office under the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as "reasonable limitations" that keep the door open to merit of every description without regard to wealth, profession, religion, nativity, or poverty; they are promoted as appropriate minimum standards for federal representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections — dependence and sympathy with the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectually secured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Election frequency should be sufficient to bind representatives to their constituents and secure their sympathy with the people. The paper reasons from experience (British, Irish, colonial) that biennial elections are adequate to maintain dependence without the dangers alleged against less frequent returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length — biennial elections justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that "biennial elections, under the federal system, cannot possibly be dangerous to the requisite dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using historical examples (House of Commons triennial/ septennial changes; colonial practices), the essay argues that two-year terms are both safe for liberty and beneficial relative to the federal government's scope and powers; biennial terms are presented as the appropriate compromise between responsiveness and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length proportional to knowledge/experience required
rubrics_metrics.description: "The period of service...ought, therefore, in all such cases, to bear some proportion to the extent of practical knowledge requisite to the due performance of the service."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because federal legislators must learn diverse state laws, interstate commerce particulars, militia regulations, and elements of foreign affairs (treaties, commercial policy, law of nations), a longer period of service (two years rather than one) better matches the practical knowledge required for effective federal legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical considerations favoring longer terms (travel, re-election costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer terms reduce the burden of travel and the impediments to suitable persons serving from distant States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance and the arrangements required of representatives from distant States make a one-year term more discouraging; two-year terms make service more feasible and reduce attrition of fit men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency as check on illicit returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Short (annual) terms can encourage "unlawful means" to obtain seats because the irregular member could hold the seat long enough to accomplish purposes before being displaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biennial elections reduce the incentive for electoral fraud in distant States because an illegitimate member would hold office longer only if the dispute resolution can keep pace; longer terms mitigate this abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment by population (same rule as direct taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The next view...relates to the appointment of its members to the several States which is to be determined by the same rule with that of direct taxes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation should be regulated by the number of people (aggregate number of inhabitants) — the same federal rule used for apportioned direct taxes — because numbers are the proper scale of representation even if imperfect as a measure of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of slaves in the census (mixed character; 3/5 compromise rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate whether slaves "ought therefore to be comprehended in estimates of taxation which are founded on property, and to be excluded from representation which is regulated by a census of persons." Federal Constitution views slaves "in the mixed character of persons and of property" and adopts a compromising expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument defends regarding slaves as inhabitants but "debased by servitude" (hence counted fractionally) because (a) state laws treat slaves partly as persons and partly as property; (b) including them for taxation but excluding for representation (or vice versa) would be inconsistent and unfair in negotiations; and (c) an agreed compromise (treating slaves as a fractional part of a person) harmonizes competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of property/wealth in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Government is instituted no less for protection of the property, than of the persons, of individuals...some attention ought, therefore, to be paid to property in the choice of those hands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because property is an object of government protection and states do not exert influence over other states as rich citizens do within a state, representation should in some measure reflect relative wealth of States (hence using population as a proxy that also correlates with wealth), securing appropriate influence to more wealthy states via greater representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same rule for representation and taxation to reduce census bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests, which will control and balance each other, and produce the requisite impartiality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the same federal rule (aggregate inhabitants) to apportion both representation and direct taxes counteracts incentives for States to manipulate counts: if representation alone governed, states would exaggerate inhabitants; if taxation alone governed, they would undercount — using the same rule balances those pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for deciding the total number of Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges against a small total: unsafe depositary of public interests; improper knowledge of local circumstances; selection from classes unsympathetic to the people; and disproportion over time as population increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing the House's size, consider (a) adequate deposit of public interests, (b) members' ability to know local circumstances of numerous constituents, (c) class-representativeness to avoid elites dominating, and (d) adjustability to population growth so initial defects do not worsen with demographic change. Comparative state practices (ratios of representatives to constituents) are used as empirical points of reference.
